title: Doctor blames death on 'excited delirium'
article: On Sept. 1, 2001 less than an hour after a delusional and psychotic Stochmal was subdued by six police officers and taken into custody after he fatally stabbed his nine-year-old son, his heart stopped. Attempts to revive the 35-year-old Regina man failed.

"In my opinion if I was to fill out the death certificate the cause of death would be excited delirium due to manic depressive psychosis," Denmark told coroner Hugh Harradance after spending most of the afternoon explaining the medical condition.

Denmark confirmed Regina pathologist Dr. Edward Jones' autopsy report, which ruled out the possibility that Stochmal died of a heart attack, from an adverse reaction to pepper spray, or was asphyxiated after being hog-tied with his face to the ground.

"There was no anatomical cause of death," Jones said, explaining after looking at the circumstances leading up to Stochmal's death he concluded the possible cause of death was excited delirium syndrome.

Psychiatrist Dr. Sanjeev Sharma, who assessed Stochmal's mood (bipolar) disorder on the afternoon of Aug. 31, concluded he was manic and experiencing some anxiety but he didn't pose a threat to himself or others, and didn't need to be hospitalized.

He told the coroner's jury Friday that mood disorders can be very unpredictable and Stochmal's mental status deteriorated very quickly on the night of Sept. 1 so that by the time he arrived at his Uplands address it appears he was delusional and responding to auditory hallucinations.
Nothing could have been done medically to treat Stochmal's psychosis until police had him under control and restrained, Sharma said, noting in his frenzied and excited state safety was a major issue.

"He needed to be contained to ensure his and other people's safety and the police officers handled the situation to the best of their ability," he said, explaining that in such an agitated or altered mental state Stochmal would not be responsive to verbal commands, or comprehend the situation or the consequences of his actions.
During his psychotic episode, an excited and extremely agitated Stochmal exhibited "super human" strength during his struggles with police as they tried to subdue and restrain him.

Denmark told the jury that as a result of his Stochmal's excited state his body produced such vast quantities of adrenalin that it set his heart racing to the point where he experienced arrhythmia, an irregular rhythmic beating of his heart causing sudden cardiac arrest.
Excited delirium, he explained, is usually seen in people experiencing a psychotic episode or a cocaine-induced psychosis and very few people who experience this condition survive.

"There is no easy answer to preventing this sort of situation," Denmark said, explaining while more training on this potential condition for police and the medical community might be beneficial, the outcome might still be the same.
